forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news.title: ‘I don’t know where the kids will go’: beloved football cage in east London to be demolished
news.summary:
Hackney council will close Keith Miller sports pitch at end of year to build urgently needed social homes

Campaigners say the loss of a much-loved football pitch in east London to a housebuilding programme will be a huge blow to the local community.

Hackney’s Keith Miller sports pitch is known locally as the “San Siro of east London” – for non-football fans, that’s the famous Milan stadium that is one of the biggest in Europe. The Hackney version, however, is due to be demolished at the end of the year so that urgently needed social homes can be built.

news_drafts.headline: Hackney defers £289m of capital spending as major programmes slip
news_drafts.lead: Hackney Council has deferred £288.5m of capital investment planned for 2026/27 to later years, with most of the money pushed back to 2027/28. The deferral signals material disruption to the council's planned spending on long-lived assets — buildings, roads and equipment — across multiple major programmes. The council's strategy to reduce temporary accommodation reliance through acquiring and refurbishing homes has accumulated £189.6m in unspent budgets, with a further £39.2m deferred from this year. Six major housing regeneration schemes show consistent patterns of unspent money: Colville Phase 2C has carried forward £42.6m, Nightingale Block E £23.4m, Kings Crescent Phase 3+4 £18.1m, Buckland Street £16.9m, Fairbank £20.1m and Wimbourne Street £15.2m. The scale and breadth of slippage across independent projects suggests a programme-wide capacity issue rather than isolated delays.

findings.paper_title: Open Appendix 1 - Summary of Re-Profiling Phase 1, Carry Forward Budget & Capital Adjustments 26-27 - Google Docs
findings.headline: Victoria House receives £29.6m budget adjustment from zero allocation, indicating new major capital commitment or mid-year reprioritisation
findings.detail: Victoria House appears in capital adjustments with a revised budget of £0 adjusted upward by £29.6m. This represents either a new capital commitment or substantial mid-year reprioritisation not captured in original budget setting. The purpose and financing of this item are not detailed in the appendix.
findings.matters: Material capital additions introduced mid-year, or previously unbudgeted commitments of this scale, indicate either changed strategic priorities or incomplete capital planning. A lender needs to establish what Victoria House represents, whether additional borrowing is required to fund it, and what impact it has on overall capital programme viability.
findings.figures: £29.6m addition, from £0 allocation to £29.6m revised budget

findings.paper_title: Open Appendix 1 - Summary of Re-Profiling Phase 1, Carry Forward Budget & Capital Adjustments 26-27 - Google Docs
findings.headline: Housing estate renewal portfolio shows sustained pattern of unspent budgets (£150m+) across multiple major schemes, indicating systemic programme delivery challenge
findings.detail: Major housing regeneration schemes display consistent carry-forward budgets across independent projects: Fairbank £20.1m, Wimbourne Street £15.2m, Buckland Street £16.9m, Kings Crescent Phase 3+4 £18.1m, Nightingale Block E £23.4m, Colville Phase 2C £42.6m. The pattern of carry-forward across multiple diverse schemes suggests a programme-wide capacity or coordination issue rather than isolated project problems.
findings.matters: Housing regeneration schemes are capital-intensive and often financed through borrowing. Systemic delays across multiple independent schemes indicate programme management risk, potential for cost escalation, and possible need for additional borrowing. The breadth of the pattern suggests a structural constraint in the council's project delivery capacity.
findings.figures: Six major schemes with £10m+ carry-forward each: Fairbank £20.1m, Wimbourne Street £15.2m, Buckland Street £16.9m, Kings Crescent £18.1m, Nightingale Block E £23.4m, Colville Phase 2C £42.6m

findings.paper_title: Open Appendix 1 - Summary of Re-Profiling Phase 1, Carry Forward Budget & Capital Adjustments 26-27 - Google Docs
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation mitigation: £39.2m deferred from 2026/27 (£34.4m investment, £4.8m acquisition) with cumulative unspent carry-forward of £189.6m
findings.detail: The council defers £34.4m of Temporary Accommodation Investment and £4.8m of TA Council Housing Acquisition from 2026/27. Cumulative carry-forward budgets stand at £121.9m and £67.7m respectively (£189.6m combined), indicating the council's core mitigation strategy—acquiring and refurbishing homes to reduce reliance on temporary accommodation—is not progressing as planned. The pattern of deferrals and accumulated unspent budget is material.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is the largest budget pressure on London councils. If capital mitigation through acquisition and refurbishment is stalling, operational TA budgets remain under pressure and threatens financial sustainability. A lender must establish whether the council has alternative mitigation strategies or faces uncontrolled budget exposure in this area.
findings.figures: Phase 1 deferrals: £34.4m (TA Investment) + £4.8m (TA Council Housing Acq) = £39.2m; cumulative carry-forward: £121.9m + £67.7m = £189.6m

findings.paper_title: Open Appendix 1 - Summary of Re-Profiling Phase 1, Carry Forward Budget & Capital Adjustments 26-27 - Google Docs
findings.headline: Council re-profiles £288.5m of capital spending from 2026/27, indicating material delivery slippage across the capital programme
findings.detail: Hackney is deferring £288.5m of capital investment planned for 2026/27 to 2027/28 and beyond in Phase 1 re-profiling. The move represents a comprehensive push-back of capital delivery, with £280.7m going to 2027/28 and only £7.8m proceeding to 2028/29. The scale and breadth of deferral signals material disruption to planned capital delivery.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage indicates project management or operational challenges. A lender needs to understand whether the council can deliver capital programmes on schedule, as deferrals affect realisation of expected benefits, cash flow forecasting, and may presage downstream cost escalation or additional borrowing.

findings.headline: Overall audit assurance has declined: only 80% of audits rated Significant or Reasonable (down from 86% prior year).
findings.detail: The proportion of audits rated Significant or Reasonable assurance has fallen from 86% in 2024/25 to 80% in 2025/26. Although the council notes different services are audited each year, this is a measurable decline in the overall control environment. Multiple audits of housing-related functions received Limited or No Assurance ratings.
findings.matters: A declining proportion of audits providing strong assurance indicates a weakening control environment. For a lender, this signals that governance is deteriorating across the council.
findings.figures: 80% Significant/Reasonable assurance (2025/26) vs 86% (2024/25); 31% Significant vs 49% Reasonable
findings.quote: The percentage of 'Significant' and 'Reasonable' assurance rated audits has slightly declined since last year (80% compared to 86%).
